title: Tico-nomics
text:
Field Note F3: World Bank Lending in Costa Rica
Working Title: Infrastructure, Reform, and Resilience: What the World Bank Has Financed in Costa Rica, 1990–2024
Research Question: - Primary: How has the sectoral and thematic distribution of World Bank lending to Costa Rica shifted across 35 years, and what do project patterns reveal about the country’s changing development priorities and World Bank strategy? - Secondary: How does Costa Rica’s lending pattern compare to its macroeconomic trajectory (growth, debt, social indicators)?

Significance
Costa Rica is a genuine development success story — a country with strong biodiversity conservation, universal health coverage, and high human development relative to income — yet it has also relied significantly on external borrowing, including from the World Bank, particularly around fiscal reform periods. The World Bank’s project-level data is publicly accessible and rich, covering project descriptions, sectors, amounts, and dates. Tracing 35 years of lending reveals which institutions and sectors the Bank (and by extension, Costa Rican governments) prioritized at each historical moment: SAPs in the 1990s, infrastructure in the 2000s, climate and education lending in the 2010s, COVID fiscal support in the 2020s.
Organizations that would value this: development institutions, Costa Rica policy researchers, civil society organizations, international development students and practitioners, researchers interested in the World Bank’s country strategy evolution.

Geographic and Temporal Scope

Unit: Project level (72 confirmed Costa Rica projects in the WB Projects API)
Geography: Costa Rica
Years: 1990–2024 (full confirmed WB portfolio)
Supplemental context: WDI economic/social indicators for Costa Rica (confirmed via wbstats)

Caveats: The 72 projects include all Bank lending instruments (investment loans, development policy loans, CAT DDOs, technical assistance). Not all “projects” are equivalent in analytical weight — a $500M DPL is very different from a $5M technical assistance grant. The project description text is rich but in English (descriptions of projects from the 1990s may be sparse). Board approval dates are available; actual disbursement schedules are not in the Projects API.

Proposed EDA
Language: R (httr, jsonlite, dplyr, ggplot2, lubridate, wbstats, stringr, scales)
R is appropriate because the analysis starts with a JSON API call, requires date handling (lubridate), text-based sector classification (stringr), and visualization with ggplot2.
Steps: 1. API pull (30 min): Use httr::GET() or jsonlite::fromJSON() to fetch all 72 Costa Rica projects. Parse JSON to data frame. Clean sector columns (sector1–5 have Name and Percent subfields). Extract board approval year using lubridate. 2. Data inspection (20 min): Check sector completeness, identify null sectors, note large vs. small projects. Log-transform loan amounts for visualization. 3. Timeline visualization (40 min): Gantt-style chart or scatter plot of project amounts over time, colored by sector. Annotate key historical events (1994 financial crisis, 2008 global crisis, 2017–2020 fiscal consolidation, COVID 2020). 4. Sector analysis (40 min): Aggregate total lending by sector across three eras (pre-2010, 2010–2019, 2020–2024). Stacked bar. Has the Bank shifted from infrastructure to DPLs, or from social to climate? 5. Instrument mix (30 min): DPLs vs. investment loans vs. technical assistance. How has the balance shifted? DPLs (budget support) often imply macro-fiscal conditionality — their frequency tells a story. 6. Supplemental macro context (30 min): Pull 3–4 WDI indicators for Costa Rica. Two-panel plot: World Bank commitment volumes by year (left axis) vs. GDP growth rate or debt-to-GDP (right axis). Does lending peak during economic stress? 7. Interpretation (60 min): Narrative connecting lending patterns to Costa Rica’s development story. Note the 5 most recent large projects (confirmed from API session): Education Results, Social Risk Management DPL, Climate Resilient Recovery, Fiscal DPL, CAT DDO — these tell a 2023–2024 policy moment story.

Originality and Contribution
Existing analyses: World Bank publishes a Costa Rica country page with portfolio summary. Academic papers analyze World Bank conditionality globally. Individual project evaluations exist. What is uncommon is a researcher doing their own data pull from the Projects API and constructing a visual narrative of a single country’s 35-year lending trajectory.
What this adds: A reproducible, researcher-constructed EDA from the Projects API — demonstrating that the researcher can work with institutional data sources, not just pre-formatted teaching datasets. The Costa Rica connection is authentic (researcher has academic and research experience in country). The analysis differs entirely from the existing Floodlines or Capital Crashpad projects.

Feasibility



Phase
Estimated Time

Most likely obstacle: Sector field parsing. The API returns sector data as JSON subobjects with Name and Percent fields; some projects have 5 sectors. Cleaning this into a flat format takes more time than expected if the JSON structure is irregular. Fallback: use only sector1 (the primary sector) if sector5 data is sparse.

Hiring Signal
Demonstrates: API data acquisition (JSON), lubridate date handling, sector classification logic, multi-indicator context building, domain knowledge about World Bank instruments (DPLs, CAT DDOs, investment lending), Costa Rica-specific knowledge.
Relevant roles: international development analyst, World Bank or IFC positions, development finance research, Central America-focused organizations, multilateral development bank support roles.

Limitations

72 projects is a small dataset. Most visualizations will have N < 100. Statistical inference is not meaningful. This is descriptive storytelling, not regression analysis.
Project amounts vs. disbursements: Board approval amounts differ from actual disbursements. DPLs (budget support) are typically drawn down quickly; investment loans may take years.
No project outcomes data. The Projects API does not include project completion ratings or outcome assessments (those are in a separate ICR database, not easily accessible).
Sector classification is coarse. The Bank’s own sector taxonomy changed over time; comparing 1995 and 2024 sectors requires care.
Puerto Rico comparison is unavailable: USVI and Puerto Rico are U.S. territories with no World Bank projects.




F3: World Bank Lending in Costa Rica
1. First action: - Open https://search.worldbank.org/api/v2/projects?format=json&countrycode=CR&rows=100&fl=id,project_name,totalamt,sector1,sector2,sector3,boardapprovaldate,closingdate,status,project_abstract - This URL is confirmed working and returns 72 projects. Copy the JSON response into a text editor to inspect the structure before writing the R code. - Secondary documentation: https://projects.worldbank.org/en/projects-operations/projects-home?lang=en
2. First inspection: - Parse JSON: count total projects (confirmed 72). Check range of board approval dates (earliest and latest project). - Inspect sector1 field — what values appear most frequently? Is sector data complete for all 72 projects? - Check the distribution of totalamt — are there large outliers (e.g., $500M DPLs)? - Note the 5 most recent projects from the confirmed API response: Education Results (2024), Social Risk Management DPL (2024), Climate Resilient Recovery (2024), Fiscal DPL (2023), CAT DDO (2023) — these are a ready-made set to profile.
3. Initial EDA checks: 1. Histogram of totalamt (log scale) — what’s the typical project size? 2. Timeline scatter: projects over time colored by sector — any visible shift? 3. Count projects by decade (1990s, 2000s, 2010s, 2020s) 4. Total lending by decade — did the Bank lend more or less over time? 5. Pull WDI GDP growth for Costa Rica: wb_data("NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG", country="CR", start_date=1990, end_date=2024) — annotate on lending timeline
4. Technical setup:
library(jsonlite); library(dplyr); library(ggplot2); library(lubridate)
library(wbstats); library(scales); library(stringr)

url <- "https://search.worldbank.org/api/v2/projects?format=json&countrycode=CR&rows=100"
raw <- fromJSON(url)
projects <- raw$projects %>% bind_rows()  # flatten list of lists to tibble
projects$board_year <- year(as.Date(projects$boardapprovaldate))
projects$totalamt <- as.numeric(projects$totalamt)
5. Feasibility test: - GO if: JSON parse works, sector1 column is populated for ≥50 of 72 projects, board approval dates span at least 1990–2023, and totalamt is non-null for the large projects. - NO-GO (reframe question) if: Sector data is so sparse that sector analysis is impossible. Fallback: reframe as a lending timeline analysis only, supplemented by WDI context, without sector decomposition.
6. Time budget: - Initial feasibility test: 20–30 minutes - Complete Field Note: 5–7 hours
7. Minimum viable deliverable: A Quarto HTML with: (a) timeline plot of WB project amounts by year, annotated with key Costa Rica events; (b) sector breakdown for the three most recent decades; (c) loan volume trend; (d) supplemental WDI macro context (GDP growth, debt); (e) 400-word interpretation connecting lending to development story. 72 projects is enough for a compelling narrative EDA even without deep statistical analysis.
8. Principal failure mode: Sector field inconsistency. The WB sector taxonomy changed multiple times between 1990 and 2024. Projects approved in 1990 may use different sector codes than 2024 projects. The fallback is to group sectors into 5–6 broad categories manually, accepting some imprecision in the early years.

F. Costa Rica’s development trajectory





Key macroeconomic and social indicators, 1990–2024. These are contextual comparisons, not evidence of causation.





GDP per capita grew from approximately $1,800 (1990) to $18,900 (2024), a 930% increase in nominal terms.
Life expectancy improved from 76.1 years (1990) to 79.3 years (2022), among the highest in Latin America.
Gini index shows moderate inequality with some reduction over the 2010s, followed by a COVID-related spike around 2020–2021.






World Bank commitment volumes indexed against GDP per capita trajectory. Both series scaled to 0–100% of their respective 1990–2024 range. Not a direct comparison.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
G. Findings and interpretation

Finding 1: The portfolio is highly concentrated in time and instrument type
More than 71% of confirmed 1990–2024 commitments were approved in just 2020–2024. This reflects the emergence of very large DPL series ($300–500M each) rather than a gradual escalation. The earlier portfolio consisted primarily of Investment Project Financing in the $15–200M range.
Why it matters: The recent shift toward large DPLs signals a change in the Bank-government relationship — from project-by-project investment toward programmatic budget support tied to policy reform. This warrants investigation into the fiscal context (Costa Rica entered a major fiscal reform process after 2018).


Finding 2: Environmental themes appear consistently, but their framing changes
Environmental and natural resource themes are present across all periods. In the 1990s–2000s, this meant biodiversity conservation and payment-for-environmental-services projects (Ecomarkets, GEF mainstreaming). By 2020–2024, the same environmental commitment is expressed through the Fiscal and Decarbonization DPL series — linking fiscal reform directly to decarbonization.
Why it matters: This suggests Costa Rica’s environmental identity has been institutionalized into its fiscal and macroeconomic policy framework, not just ring-fenced in project-level investments. Whether the Bank is responding to Costa Rican government priorities or helping shape them is a question worth investigating.


Finding 3: A notable gap in the 2013–2019 period (partially an artifact)
The confirmed time series shows almost no projects between 2012 and 2020. Some of this gap is real (World Bank may have had lower engagement during Costa Rica’s pre-reform fiscal stress), but some is an artifact of 16 projects with missing dates. Further investigation — via the WB project website or a different API query — is needed to accurately populate this period.
Why it matters: If Costa Rica was indeed under-served by Bank lending in 2013–2019, this would coincide with the country’s fiscal deterioration (deficits widened substantially from ~3% to ~8% of GDP over this period). The absence of Bank engagement, followed by a massive surge in DPL budget support post-2020, would tell a coherent story about the Bank as a lender-of-last-resort for fiscal adjustment.


Finding 4: Project scale has increased dramatically
The median confirmed in-scope project commitment is $158M. But that median is pulled down by many small projects. The five largest projects are all $200M+, all approved after 2009, and all either DPLs or large infrastructure operations.
Why it matters: This mirrors a global trend in World Bank operations toward fewer but larger operations. Smaller countries like Costa Rica may get fewer but costlier loans, concentrating the policy leverage (and conditionality) in a smaller number of very large transactions.


Finding 5: Costa Rica’s economic trajectory is largely independent of lending volume
GDP per capita and life expectancy improved steadily throughout the period, regardless of lending volume. The Gini index shows modest variation. The largest World Bank commitments do not obviously coincide with turning points in development indicators.
Why it matters: This is consistent with the Bank’s role as a supplemental financier in a middle-income country, not a transformative external actor. Costa Rica’s development record is predominantly domestically driven. The Bank’s leverage is likely concentrated in specific policy reform windows (2009, 2020–2023) rather than broad development outcomes.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
section: H. What the data tells us — and what it cannot
text:
H. What the data tells us — and what it cannot
What the data tells us:

The World Bank has committed approximately $3.3B to 25 confirmed 1990–2024 Costa Rica projects (more if missing-date projects are included).
The portfolio has shifted from project-level investments in transport, education, and environment to very large budget-support operations focused on fiscal management and decarbonization.
Environmental and climate themes are embedded across every lending period.
Disaster risk and resilience language is a recent addition to the portfolio vocabulary.

What the data cannot tell us:

Whether World Bank projects achieved their stated objectives.
Whether Bank conditions influenced Costa Rican policy decisions.
The nature or magnitude of the 2013–2019 gap (missing-date problem).
How this portfolio compares to other middle-income IBRD borrowers.
Whether lending caused, responded to, or was independent of macroeconomic changes.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
I. Recommended next steps

Resolve missing-date projects: Query the World Bank project website directly for the 16 projects to recover approval dates and complete the timeline.
Investigate the 2013–2019 gap: Research whether Costa Rica genuinely had a lean period with the Bank and understand the fiscal context (SAL-era debt, 2018 fiscal reform crisis).
Explore the Decarbonization DPL series in depth: The three Fiscal and Decarbonization DPLs (2020–2023) are the dominant story of the recent portfolio. What policy conditions did they include? What has the fiscal reform achieved?
Add inflation adjustment: Deflate nominal amounts using the US GDP deflator or CPI to enable more accurate cross-period comparisons.
Comparative context: How does Costa Rica’s portfolio composition compare to comparable IBRD borrowers (Panama, Dominican Republic, Colombia)? The World Bank API makes this comparison feasible.
Primary sources: Supplement this quantitative portrait with project assessment reports (ICRs and ICRRs) from the World Bank’s Operations Portal for the major projects.

title: The World Bank in Costa Rica
text:
From 1990 to 2024, the World Bank approved 25 projects in Costa Rica, committing approximately $3.3B in IBRD lending (nominal US dollars at time of commitment).
This portfolio traces a country navigating structural adjustment, infrastructure investment, fiscal reform, environmental leadership, and pandemic response — all while maintaining one of Latin America’s strongest human development records.
This site presents an exploratory, descriptive analysis of that portfolio. It is not a causal study.



Primary: How has the sectoral and thematic distribution of World Bank lending to Costa Rica changed from 1990 to 2024, and what do these patterns reveal about evolving development priorities?
Secondary: How do changes in development financing relate chronologically to Costa Rica’s broader economic and social trajectory?

title: Missing Date Investigation
text:
2. Date recovery method

What was tried
The original data used the World Bank Projects Search API V2 (search.worldbank.org/api/v2/projects), which returns boardapprovaldate as null for these 16 projects.
Three additional sources were checked in sequence:

WB Project Detail Pages (projects.worldbank.org/en/projects-operations/project-detail/{id}) — These are JavaScript single-page applications (SPAs). The raw HTML does not contain the project data; it is loaded by Angular components from the API. Not suitable for scraping.
WB Document API (search.worldbank.org/api/v2/wds) — Returns document metadata with document disclosure dates (docdt), not board approval dates. Used to estimate approximate preparation periods but not to recover specific dates.
WB Projects API V3 (search.worldbank.org/api/v3/projects) and WB Bulk Excel Download (search.worldbank.org/api/v3/projects/all.xlsx, downloaded 2026-10-30) — Both V3 and Excel contained boardapprovaldate for 15 of the 16 projects. V3 API and Excel agreed on all 15 dates with zero discrepancies.



Source reliability

V3 API and bulk Excel (2026-10-30) are two delivery channels of the same World Bank database.
Agreement across both independent output channels for all 15 recovered dates gives high confidence that these are the WB’s authoritative board approval dates for those projects.
Three dates fall on June 30 (fiscal year end): P006930, P006950, P006951. These are a common WB convention for projects without a precise approval date recorded in the system. The year is likely correct; the June 30 date is a fiscal year approximation.
P169724 (Learning for All, $100M, Dropped) has no date in either V3 or Excel. This is the only genuinely unresolvable case.

Verdict
The apparent 2013–2019 gap is both a partial artifact and a real pattern:
It is partly a missing-data artifact: - P122265 ($200M, Health Networks APL) was approved 2014-07-03 and simply lacked a date in the V2 API. Adding it places a substantial commitment in 2014. - P163431 ($0) and P167926 ($0) fill 2018 with two genuine project approvals — though neither had positive IBRD financing.
It is also a real pattern: - Even with all recovered dates, 2013, 2015, 2016, 2017, and 2019 still show no confirmed positive IBRD financing commitments. - P169724 ($100M Learning for All, Dropped) remains unresolved. If it was approved in 2015–2019, it would fill part of the remaining gap. Its document evidence (preparation docs from 2019–2020) suggests it may have been Dropped before the board, meaning no approval date exists. - The 2015–2019 financing gap appears real: Costa Rica did not receive substantial new IBRD investment loans during this period. The evidence is consistent with lower Bank engagement during Costa Rica’s fiscal deterioration (deficit widening from ~3% to ~8% GDP, 2015–2019).


Recommendation
The 2013–2019 gap can be presented as follows:

“World Bank lending to Costa Rica was sparse between 2013 and 2019 by both project count and financing volume. The $200M Health Networks APL (2014) was board-approved during this period but was subsequently dropped; no large investment or policy loans were committed between 2015 and 2019. The pattern is consistent with lower Bank engagement during Costa Rica’s pre-reform fiscal stress, though the evidence does not allow a causal claim.”

This framing: - Acknowledges the one meaningful project in 2014 (now visible with recovered dates) - Accurately reports the 2015–2019 financing absence - Avoids asserting causation while noting the fiscal context as potentially relevant - Notes the $100M unresolved project without manufacturing a conclusion

Sector allocations: When sector percentage data is available and sums to approximately 100%, project financing is allocated proportionally across sectors. For example, a $100M project where 60% goes to Public Administration and 40% to Transportation contributes $60M and $40M respectively to sector totals. This avoids double-counting project financing.
When percentages are unavailable or do not sum correctly, projects are included in sector counts but excluded from allocated financing totals.

Overall verdict: Proceed with modifications
The core project-level data is sufficient to support a meaningful exploratory analysis of World Bank lending in Costa Rica from 1990 to 2024.
Modifications relative to original scope:

Time series gap: The 16 missing-date projects create an apparent gap in 2013–2019 activity. All charts note this limitation explicitly.
Sector analysis limited: Only 3 sector slots captured; most recent projects lack sector data. Sector analysis is indicative, not complete.
Nominal amounts only: No inflation adjustment is applied. Cross-period comparisons of dollar amounts should be treated as approximations.
Adult literacy excluded: Insufficient data points.
Gini treated carefully: Annual data is available, but trend interpretation should be tempered by awareness of survey-to-survey variation.

The analysis proceeds with these limitations documented throughout.
